Saladin. Born eleven thirty-seven, died eleven ninety-three, born Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi, a Kurdish-born Muslim military commander and diplomat who united the fragmented Islamic world, defeated the Crusaders, and retook Jerusalem. His chivalry and strategic brilliance earned respect from both Christian and Muslim contemporaries, and he became the defining figure of the later Crusades, embodying Islamic resistance and the eventual reversals of Crusader territorial gains.

Saladin rose from service in the army of Nur ad-Din, the Zengid ruler, and eventually seized control of Egypt, establishing the Ayyubid dynasty and using Egypt's wealth to finance a unified campaign against the Crusader kingdoms. His great victory at the Battle of Hattin in July of eleven eighty-seven destroyed the principal Crusader field army, killing or capturing thousands. The decisive defeat forced Crusader garrisons to surrender across the Levant.

Saladin retook Jerusalem in October of eleven eighty-seven, ending nearly a century of Crusader rule. His conduct offered safe passage to Christian civilians and treated the city's Christian shrines with respect, contrasting sharply with the brutality of the First Crusade's conquest in ten ninety-nine and enhancing his reputation as a civilized warrior. His military reforms included standardizing armies, establishing professional soldier corps—the Mamluks—and investing in fortifications and naval power. He recognized that defeating the Crusaders required sustained military organization, not just battlefield victories.

Saladin's diplomacy was as important as his warfare. He played Crusader states against each other, negotiated truces and ransoms, and maintained correspondence with European rulers. He projected strength while avoiding unnecessary bloodshed. Though the Third Crusade from eleven eighty-nine to eleven ninety-two arrived in response to his victories, led by Richard the Lionheart, Saladin held the line. The resulting Treaty of Jaffa in eleven ninety-two established a truce: Crusaders retained coastal enclaves, but Muslim control of Jerusalem and the interior was secure. He shares connections with the Crusades, the religious conflict that defined his military career, with the Battle of Hattin, his greatest victory and the turning point of the Crusades, with the Ayyubid Dynasty, the dynasty he founded that ruled Egypt and the Levant, and with Jerusalem, the holy city he reconquered from the Crusaders.
